children.name: California State Legislature
children.description: The Legislature passes the actual law: the Budget Act, “budget bill juniors” that amend it during the year, and trailer bills. Committee staff publish their own summaries, with their own category conventions.

children.name: Budget Act (the enacted budget bill)
children.description: The legal appropriations, item by item, in whole dollars, with provisional language. Amounts differ from the budget display, which also shows non-Budget Act (continuous/statutory) spending.

Highlights of the Governor’s Budget / May Revision
State Controller’s Office
children.description: The Controller pays the bills and keeps the books, so it reports what was actually spent and received, on two different accounting bases.

children.name: Annual Comprehensive Financial Report (ACFR, GAAP basis)
children.description: Audited, accrual-basis statements, organized by government-wide/fund statements rather than budget departments. Will not match the budget figures.

children.name: Budgetary/Legal Basis Annual Report
children.description: Actuals on the same (modified cash) basis as the Budget Act.

children.name: ByTheNumbers open data (local government finances)
children.description: Cities, counties and special districts: where much state money ends up as local assistance.

children.name: State Treasurer’s Office
children.description: Issues and tracks the State’s debt: the other side of “bond funds”.

children.name: State bond programs, disclosures and reports
FI$Cal (Financial Information System for California)
children.description: The State’s accounting system. Its transparency portal publishes transaction-level spending: vendor payments, not budget programs.

children.name: Expenditure downloads (transactions)
children.description: Coded by FI$Cal business unit/account, not by the budget display’s program codes; some departments are not on FI$Cal.

children.name: Legislative Analyst’s Office (non-partisan analysis)
children.description: Analysis, not official budget data: LAO re-estimates revenues and re-groups spending, so its numbers often differ from DOF’s on purpose.

children.name: 2026 budget publications (overview of the Governor’s Budget, May Revision, spending plan)
California Department of Education (Proposition 98)
children.description: Roughly 40% of the General Fund is governed by the Proposition 98 school-funding guarantee, which is recalculated and certified years after the budget passes.

children.name: Proposition 98 guarantee & certification
children.description: The guarantee for a year keeps changing until it is certified, so the “Prop 98” split in any one budget is an estimate.

children.name: Retirement systems (CalPERS / CalSTRS)
children.description: State pension contributions appear as budget lines, but the trust funds themselves are “nongovernmental cost funds” and their finances are reported separately.

children.name: Tax agencies (FTB / CDTFA)
children.description: The agencies that collect the money. Their statistics are on a collections basis, while Schedule 8 is on an accrual/budget basis.

children.name: Franchise Tax Board data, reports & plans (income taxes)
CDTFA open data portal (sales & excise taxes)
Oversight & open data
children.description: Audits of how budgeted money was used, and the State’s general open-data portal.

painPoints.title: The detail only exists as PDF
painPoints.body: The JSON API stops at program level and fund totals. Subprograms and elements, spending by category and object (salaries, rent, grants…), Budget Act appropriation items and fund condition statements are only printed in the department detail PDFs, so they have to be parsed out of page layouts.
painPoints.example: 201 department PDFs (1,613 pages) parsed for this dataset.

painPoints.title: Thousands, millions, billions — and whole dollars
painPoints.body: Summary Schedules and most API endpoints print thousands of dollars; the API’s General Fund “sankey”, the Summary Charts, Schedule 5B (cash) and Schedule 12A (spending limit) print millions; the narrative chapters round to tenths of a billion; the Budget Act itself appropriates whole dollars. Every comparison needs a unit conversion and a rounding tolerance.
painPoints.example: General Fund spending is 251,477 in the sankey endpoint (millions) and 251,477,209 in the statistics endpoint (thousands).

painPoints.title: Some figures are only pictures
painPoints.body: The Budget Summary “Summary Charts” chapter (e.g. the General Fund Budget Summary table and the Proposition 98 split) is a PDF of images: there is no text layer to extract. Those numbers have to be typed in by hand and cross-checked.
painPoints.example: 35 figures in this dataset were transcribed by hand from chart images (millions).

painPoints.title: The May Revision is published differently
painPoints.body: For the May Revision, ebudget publishes department totals only (the statistics/revised endpoint). There are no May department detail PDFs and no May Summary Schedules — its General Fund summary is only in the Summary Charts images; the item-level changes are in DOF’s separate May letters on dof.ca.gov.
painPoints.example: https://ebudget.ca.gov/2026-27/pdf/Revised/BudgetSummary/BS_SCH1.pdf answered 404 when checked (Nov 2026); so did the Revised department PDFs.

painPoints.title: Two different agency codes for the same department
painPoints.body: Each department record has an org agency code (which folder its PDF is filed under) and a web agency code (which agency it is displayed under, and what the statistics endpoint groups by). They usually match, but not always, and some display agencies have no PDF folder at all.
painPoints.example: 29 of 239 department records disagree. 0521 Secretary for Transportation Agency: shown under agency 2500, but its PDF lives in folder GovernorsBudget/0010/. Display agencies 6013 (Higher Education) and 6010 (K thru 12 Education) have no PDF folder: their departments are filed under 6000 (Education), 0010 (Legislative, Judicial, and Executive).

painPoints.title: Schedules identify agencies by name, not code
painPoints.body: Schedule 9 (spending by agency and fund type) prints agency names without codes, so it has to be matched to the API by normalized name, falling back to a vote of its department codes.

painPoints.title: The API and the PDFs don’t always agree
painPoints.body: The same department’s totals are published twice — by the JSON API and in its PDF — and occasionally differ (different program roll-ups, capital outlay counted in one but not the other). This explorer uses the API figure for totals and shows any difference as an explicit residual.
painPoints.example: 5 mismatches in this dataset, e.g. “3340: fund total 180932/217206/202707 != programs+infrastructure 180932/223602/202707”.

painPoints.title: Not every PDF has the same sections
painPoints.body: Department PDFs follow a common template, but sections are omitted when a department has nothing to report — and sometimes when it does — so every parser has to cope with missing tables.
painPoints.example: 4 department PDFs have no “Detailed Expenditures by Program” section (9625, 9650, 6645, 0150).

painPoints.title: “Enacted” documents that are still the January version
painPoints.body: Not every schedule is updated at each stage. In the Enacted Budget folder, Schedules 2, 3, 5B and 12B are still titled “at 2026-27 Governor’s Budget”, next to Schedules 1, 4, 6, 8–11 and 12A titled “at 2026 Budget Act”.
painPoints.example: Observed in the Enacted BudgetSummary folder, Nov 2026.

painPoints.title: “All funds” counts some money twice
painPoints.body: ebudget’s “all funds” total includes reimbursements (one department paying another) and nongovernmental cost funds (pension trusts, university own funds, local property tax). Totals that do and don’t include them circulate side by side.
painPoints.example: $793.7 billion “all funds” includes $45.5 billion of reimbursements and $209.2 billion of nongovernmental cost funds.

painPoints.title: Spending that belongs to no department page
painPoints.body: Statewide items (general obligation bond debt service, employee compensation augmentations, Prop 98 reconciliation…) are in agency totals but are hidden from the department listing (displayOnWebFlg = N) and have no detail PDF.

painPoints.title: Fund condition statements are published twice
painPoints.body: Each special fund’s balance sheet appears inside the administering department’s detail PDF and again in a separate {org}FCS.pdf — and Schedule 10 summarizes them a third time. Printed statements don’t always add up.
painPoints.example: 108 separate FCS PDFs fetched. fund 0367: FCS (0855 PDF p3) does not balance: begin+revenues/transfers-expenditures 115430/105658/104804 vs printed fund balance 110544/110544/104804

painPoints.title: An undocumented API
painPoints.body: ebudget’s JSON API has no public documentation; endpoints were reverse-engineered from the site’s JavaScript bundle. Its URL prefix changed between years (“publication” up to 2025-26, “budget” from 2026-27), unknown codes answer with a JSON HTTP 500, and the publication index (home/getLink) returns JSON text split across an array of strings that must be joined and parsed again.

painPoints.title: Every number has three versions per publication
painPoints.body: Each publication restates three fiscal years: past-year actuals (2024-25), current-year estimates (2025-26) and the budget year (2026-27). The current year is re-estimated in every publication, so “2025-26 spending” has a different value in each.

painPoints.title: Revenue and spending don’t cover the same money
painPoints.body: Schedule 8 revenue covers only state funds (General Fund and special funds). Federal funds and bond proceeds are in total spending but not in revenue, and transfers/loans move money between funds without being revenue or spending.

painPoints.title: Budget basis vs. accounting basis vs. cash
painPoints.body: The budget (DOF), the Controller’s audited statements (GAAP), the Controller’s cash reports, FI$Cal transactions and the tax agencies’ collections each use a different basis and classification, so their totals legitimately differ.

painPoints.title: Key facts only exist in prose
painPoints.body: The size of the budget problem and how it was solved are only stated in the narrative chapters (“$X billion”), and the Enacted Budget Summary prints no single table of solutions — so figures are quoted from text and cross-checked against the schedules.

notes: Files, bytes and pages are measured from the ETL download cache (data-raw/); the same document cached by two ETLs is counted once.
“Cited by” counts the source references (SourceRef) attached to nodes in this explorer’s data files; per-fund revenue nodes derived from Fund Condition Statements are counted against that series.
Sources marked “not used” are listed for completeness. Links marked “unverified” could not be checked automatically (the site blocks scripted requests).
